definition: Request for Comments: a numbered document published by the IETF. Internet standards such as HTTP, DNS and SMTP are written down as RFCs, and a protocol is often named by its RFC number.
example: RFC 9112 defines the HTTP/1.1 wire format; RFC 1035 defines the DNS message format.

definition: The Internet Engineering Task Force: the open standards body that develops and publishes most internet protocol specifications as RFCs.
example: HTTP/2, QUIC and DNSSEC were all standardised through IETF working groups.

definition: Version 1.1 of HTTP: a text protocol in which each request and response is a start line, header lines ending in CRLF, a blank line and an optional body, sent over a TCP byte stream. Connections are persistent by default.
example: GET / HTTP/1.1 followed by Host: example.com and a blank line is a complete HTTP/1.1 request.

definition: The earlier 1996 version of HTTP. By default it closed the TCP connection after each response, and the Host header was not required.

The second major version of HTTP. It keeps HTTP methods, status codes and headers but sends them as binary frames, multiplexing many streams over one TCP connection and compressing headers with HPACK.
example: A browser can fetch 50 images over one HTTP/2 connection, each on its own stream.

definition: The version of HTTP that runs over QUIC instead of TCP. Each request uses its own QUIC stream, so a lost packet delays only the streams whose data it carried, and headers are compressed with QPACK.
example: A client that sees Alt-Svc: h3=":443" may try HTTP/3 on UDP port 443.

definition: A connection that delivers an ordered sequence of bytes with no built-in message boundaries. TCP is a byte stream, so an application protocol such as HTTP/1.1 must mark where each of its own messages starts and ends.
example: Two HTTP responses sent back to back may arrive in a single recv() call, or one response may be split across three.

definition: The rules that tell a receiver where one message ends and the next begins on a byte stream, for example a length field, a delimiter or closing the connection. Two parsers that frame the same bytes differently are the root of smuggling attacks.
example: HTTP/1.1 frames a body with Content-Length, chunked encoding or connection close.

definition: Carriage return followed by line feed: the two bytes 0D 0A (written \r\n in code) that end each line in text protocols such as HTTP/1.1, SMTP and IMAP. An empty line, CRLF on its own, ends the header section.
example: A HTTP/1.1 header block ends with \r\n\r\n: the CRLF of the last header line plus an empty line.

definition: The first line of an HTTP/1.1 message: a request line in a request, or a status line in a response.
The first line of an HTTP/1.1 request: the method, the request target and the protocol version, separated by single spaces and ended by CRLF.
example: GET /search?q=tcp HTTP/1.1 is a request line.

definition: The first line of an HTTP/1.1 response: the protocol version, a three-digit status code and an optional reason phrase.
example: HTTP/1.1 200 OK is a status line.

definition: The part of an HTTP request line that names the resource, usually a path and optional query such as /search?q=tcp.
The verb at the start of an HTTP request that says what the client wants done, such as GET (fetch), POST (submit), HEAD (headers only) or CONNECT (open a tunnel).
The HTTP method for retrieving a resource. It is defined as safe, so it should not change server state, and a GET request normally has no body.
example: Following a link makes the browser send a GET request.

definition: The HTTP method for submitting data, such as a form or an upload, for the server to process. It is not a safe method, because it may change server state.
example: Submitting a bank transfer form typically sends a POST.

definition: The HTTP method that asks for the same headers a GET would return, but no body. A response to HEAD never has a body, even if it carries Content-Length.
example: A client can send HEAD /big.iso to learn the file size without downloading 4.7 GB.

definition: The HTTP method that asks a proxy to open a raw TCP tunnel to another host. After a 2xx response the connection stops carrying HTTP and simply relays bytes, which is how HTTPS passes through many forward proxies.
example: CONNECT example.com:443 HTTP/1.1 asks the proxy for a tunnel to port 443.

definition: An HTTP method defined as read-only, so a request should not change server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE. SameSite=Lax relies on this, which is why state changes must not happen on GET.
A Name: value line in an HTTP message that carries metadata about the message or its content. Names are case-insensitive, so Content-Length and content-length are the same field.
example: Host: example.com and Content-Type: text/html are header fields.

definition: The HTTP request header that names the host the client wants, such as Host: example.com. It is mandatory in HTTP/1.1 and lets one IP address serve many websites; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry it as :authority.
One of many websites served from the same IP address and port. The server picks which site to serve from the Host header (or TLS SNI).
example: shop.example and blog.example can both live on 192.0.2.10:443.

definition: The request header that identifies the client software and version, such as curl/8.5.0 or a browser string.
The request header listing the media types the client can handle; */* means any type.
The header naming the media type of the body, such as text/html, application/json or application/grpc, so the receiver knows how to interpret the bytes.
The header giving the exact size of the message body in bytes. With no transfer coding, the receiver reads exactly that many bytes after the blank line, which is how it knows where the body ends.
example: Content-Length: 1256 means 1,256 body bytes follow the headers.

definition: The HTTP/1.1 header listing codings applied to the body for transport. Its main use is Transfer-Encoding: chunked; if present it overrides Content-Length. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 forbid it.

An HTTP/1.1 way to send a body of unknown length: a series of chunks, each preceded by its size in hexadecimal and a CRLF, ending with a chunk of size 0. It lets a server stream a response without closing the connection.
example:
7
Mozilla
0

 carries the 7-byte body Mozilla.

definition: Base-16 notation, using the digits 0 to 9 and A to F (worth 10 to 15). Each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, so a byte is two hex digits; a prefix 0x often marks a hex number.
example: Hex 11 is 1 × 16 + 1 = 17, and 0xFF is 255.

definition: Optional name=value metadata after a chunk size, such as 7;name=value. Receivers must parse and limit them but ignore extensions they do not recognise.

Header fields sent after the body instead of before it, for values only known at the end, such as a checksum or a final status. HTTP/1.1 sends them after the 0 chunk; HTTP/2 sends them as a final HEADERS frame. gRPC puts its call status in trailers.
example: grpc-status: 0 arrives as a trailer after all response messages.

definition: A small value computed from data so the receiver can detect accidental corruption by recomputing it and comparing.
End of file: the condition a reader sees when the other side has closed its sending direction, so no more bytes will arrive. For a socket, recv() returning zero bytes signals EOF.
The operating-system interface a program uses to send and receive network data. A TCP socket gives the program a byte stream to read with recv() and write with send().
example: socket.create_connection(("example.com", 80)) opens a TCP socket in Python.

definition: The socket call that returns whatever bytes have arrived so far, up to a requested maximum. It does not respect application message boundaries: one call may return part of a message or several messages.
An HTTP connection that stays open after a response so further requests can reuse it, saving a new TCP (and TLS) handshake. It is the default in HTTP/1.1; Connection: close opts out.
The HTTP/1.1 header option saying the sender will close the connection after this message, so it will not be reused.

An HTTP/1.1 response whose body ends only when the server closes the connection, used when there is no Content-Length or chunked framing. It is fragile because a premature close looks the same as a complete body.
The optional content after the blank line that ends the headers, such as an HTML page or uploaded file. Framing rules decide how long it is.
An HTTP status code from 100 to 199. It is provisional: it is sent before the final response and never has a body.
example: 100 Continue tells a client to go ahead and send its request body.

definition: An interim response telling a client that sent Expect: 100-continue to go ahead and send its request body. It lets a server reject a large upload before the bytes are sent.
An interim response confirming that the connection is switching to another protocol, such as WebSocket, as the client requested.
The HTTP status code for a successful request. gRPC uses 200 even for failed calls and reports the real outcome in trailers.
A success status meaning there is no body to send. Like HEAD responses and 304, it never has a body whatever its headers say.
A response telling the client its cached copy is still current, so no body is sent.
The status code for a request the server cannot or will not process because it is malformed, such as an HTTP/1.1 request with no Host header.
The status code meaning the request lacks valid authentication credentials.
The status code meaning the request body is larger than the server will accept.

The three-digit number in an HTTP response that reports the result. The first digit gives the class: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry it in the :status pseudo-header.
A connection that an intermediary relays as raw bytes in both directions without interpreting them, for example after a successful CONNECT.
Any program between client and server that forwards HTTP messages, such as a proxy, gateway or load balancer. Each one is a separate hop that parses and may re-frame the message.

A server that receives requests and forwards them on, either for clients (forward proxy) or in front of servers (reverse proxy). A proxy that parses HTTP differently from the server behind it can enable smuggling.

In a web deployment, the front end is the first server a request reaches (a proxy, CDN or load balancer) and the back end is the application server it forwards to. They often share reused connections.

An attack in which a front end and back end disagree about where a request ends, so attacker bytes hidden in one request are treated by the back end as the start of the next. It can poison caches, bypass access controls and capture other users' requests.
example: A request with both Content-Length: 13 and Transfer-Encoding: chunked can leave 8 bytes in the back end's buffer.

definition: The request-smuggling variant where the front end frames by Content-Length (CL) and the back end by Transfer-Encoding (TE). TE.CL is the reverse.
Rules that decide which users or clients may reach which resources, often enforced at a front-end proxy.
Getting a shared HTTP cache to store a harmful response under a normal URL, so later users receive it. Request smuggling is one way to do it.

Sending several requests on one connection without waiting for each response. In HTTP/1.1 responses must return in request order, so one slow response delays the rest; SFTP and BitTorrent pipeline requests that carry IDs or offsets instead.
example: Pipelining /slow, /a and /b means /b cannot arrive before /slow finishes.

definition: Delay caused when an item at the front of an ordered queue holds up everything behind it, even items that are ready. HTTP/1.1 pipelining has it at the application level; HTTP/2 over TCP has it at the transport level when one packet is lost.
The opening exchange of messages that sets up a connection or session before data flows, such as TCP's SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK or the TLS key exchange. Each handshake costs at least one round trip.
example: A new HTTPS connection over TCP and TLS 1.3 needs two round trips before the first request.

definition: A protocol in which each request is understood on its own, with no memory of earlier requests. HTTP semantics are stateless, which is why cookies were added to carry state.
A small name=value pair a server asks the browser to store with Set-Cookie and send back in the Cookie header on later matching requests. Cookies carry sessions and preferences.
example: Cookie: sid=a3f9; theme=dark sends two cookies.

definition: The response header that creates or updates a cookie, with its name, value and attributes such as Path, Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite. Each cookie needs its own Set-Cookie line.
A cookie with neither Expires nor Max-Age, deleted when the browser session ends. Also used loosely for the cookie that holds a login session ID.

The settings after a cookie's name=value in Set-Cookie, such as Expires, Max-Age, Domain, Path, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite and Partitioned. They control lifetime and where the cookie is sent; they are never sent back to the server.
Cookie attributes setting its lifetime: Expires gives a date, Max-Age a number of seconds, and Max-Age wins if both appear. Max-Age=0 with a matching name, domain and path deletes a cookie.
example: Max-Age=3600 keeps the cookie for one hour.

definition: The cookie attribute that widens its scope to a domain and all its subdomains. Omitting it is stricter: the cookie is then host-only.
example: Domain=example.com sends the cookie to example.com, www.example.com and promo.example.com.

definition: A cookie set without a Domain attribute. The browser sends it only to the exact host that set it, not to subdomains or sibling hosts.
example: A host-only cookie from app.example.com is not sent to x.app.example.com.

definition: The cookie attribute limiting which URL paths receive the cookie. It is not a security boundary, because script on the same origin can still reach the cookie.
The cookie attribute telling the browser to send the cookie only over connections it considers secure, normally HTTPS.
The cookie attribute that hides the cookie from non-HTTP APIs such as document.cookie, so injected script cannot read it directly. Script can still make requests that carry it.

The cookie attribute controlling whether the cookie is sent on cross-site requests. Strict sends it only same-site; Lax also on top-level navigations with safe methods such as GET; None sends it cross-site and requires Secure.
example: With SameSite=Lax, a cross-site form POST to your bank does not carry your session cookie.

definition: A cookie with the Partitioned attribute, stored separately for each top-level site that embeds the setting site, so it cannot be used to track a user across sites. It requires Secure.

A special start to a cookie name that makes supporting browsers enforce rules: __Secure- cookies must be Secure and set from HTTPS; __Host- cookies must also have Path=/ and no Domain, so they are locked to one host.
The IETF draft revising RFC 6265, the cookie specification. It adds SameSite, cookie prefixes and default Lax-style behaviour.
The scheme, host and port of a URL, such as https://app.example.com:443. Browsers isolate script and data by origin.
example: https://a.example.com and https://b.example.com are different origins.

definition: For cookies, the scheme plus the registrable domain (eTLD+1). Two hosts are same-site if those match, even when they are different origins.
example: https://shop.example.co.uk and https://api.example.co.uk are the same site.

definition: A public suffix (effective top-level domain, such as .com or .co.uk) plus one more label, such as example.co.uk. It is the unit browsers use for "site".
A domain under which anyone can register names, such as com, co.uk or github.io. Browsers refuse cookies scoped to a public suffix, so one tenant cannot set cookies for all the others.
A domain name under another, such as api.example.com under example.com. Two subdomains of the same parent are siblings.
A navigation that changes the URL in the browser's address bar, such as clicking a link, as opposed to loading an image, iframe or fetch request inside a page.
An HTML element that embeds another web page inside the current one.
The browser JavaScript API for making HTTP requests from a page.
The browser JavaScript property that reads and writes the current page's non-HttpOnly cookies.
The name for the local machine itself, usually 127.0.0.1 or ::1. Browsers may treat it as secure even without HTTPS.
A cookie sent to a site other than the one in the address bar, for example an embedded advertiser. Browsers increasingly block or partition them.
A setting on a browser request that says whether cookies and other credentials may be attached, for example omit, same-origin or include in fetch.
A response header that tells the browser to delete stored data, such as cookies or cache, for the site. Clear-Cookie is not a real header.
The software acting for the user, usually a browser. Standards say what a user agent must or may do, and real browsers add their own policies.
The header naming a compression applied to the content itself, such as gzip or br (Brotli). It is a different layer from transfer coding.
A pre-production copy of a service used for testing, often less carefully secured than production.
A program design that is always in one of a fixed set of states and moves between them as input arrives. Robust parsers are state machines, because input can arrive in arbitrary slices.
The optional human-readable text after an HTTP/1.1 status code, such as OK or Not Found. Clients must not rely on it.

The four values that identify a TCP or UDP flow: source IP address, source port, destination IP address and destination port. Changing any of them looks like a new flow to TCP and to most load balancers.
The basic unit of HTTP/2: a 9-byte header (24-bit length, 8-bit type, 8-bit flags, 31-bit stream ID) followed by a payload. QUIC also carries frames, inside its packets.

An independent, ordered sequence of frames inside one connection, usually carrying one request and its response. Many streams interleave on one connection; HTTP/2 client streams have odd IDs, and stream 0 is the connection itself.

The number identifying a stream. In HTTP/2 it is 31 bits, odd for client-initiated and even for server-initiated streams; in QUIC its two low bits encode who opened it and whether it is bidirectional.
Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation: a TLS extension in which client and server agree which protocol will run over the connection, such as h2 for HTTP/2 or h3 for HTTP/3, during the handshake.

The fixed 24-byte string PRI * HTTP/2.0

SM

 that an HTTP/2 client sends first, followed by a SETTINGS frame. An HTTP/1.1 server receiving it by mistake fails cleanly.

The HTTP/2 frame (type 0x4, always on stream 0) that sets connection parameters such as the maximum frame size, initial stream window and maximum concurrent streams. The receiver acknowledges it with the ACK flag.
example: SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE may be raised from 16,384 up to 16,777,215 bytes.

definition: The HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 frame type that carries body bytes. In HTTP/2 only DATA payloads count against flow-control windows.
The HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 frame type that carries a compressed block of header fields, starting a request or response, or carrying trailers.
The HTTP/2 frame that cancels a single stream immediately without closing the connection. Abuse of it caused the 2023 Rapid Reset attack.
The HTTP/2 frame a server used to announce a response it would push before the client asked. Chrome disabled server push by default in 2022.
The HTTP/2 frame for measuring round-trip time and checking that a connection is alive; the peer echoes it with the ACK flag. gRPC keepalives use it.
The HTTP/2 frame that starts a graceful shutdown. It reports the highest stream ID the sender may have processed, so the peer knows which requests are safe to retry elsewhere.
The HTTP/2 frame a receiver sends to give the sender more flow-control credit, for one stream or the whole connection.
The HTTP/2 frame that carries the rest of a header block too large for one HEADERS frame.
The original HTTP/2 frame (type 0x2) for expressing stream dependencies and weights, now deprecated in favour of the priority header.
The HTTP/2 flag (0x1 on DATA or HEADERS) meaning the sender has finished sending on this stream.
The HTTP/2 flag (0x4) on a HEADERS or CONTINUATION frame meaning the header block is complete.
The 0x1 flag on an HTTP/2 SETTINGS or PING frame marking it as an acknowledgement of one the peer sent.
The 8-bit field in an HTTP/2 frame header holding type-specific on/off bits, such as END_STREAM (0x1) and END_HEADERS (0x4). Several flags combine by adding them: 0x05 is both.
The encoded set of header fields carried in HEADERS (and any CONTINUATION) frames, compressed with HPACK in HTTP/2 or QPACK in HTTP/3.

An HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 field whose name starts with a colon and replaces the HTTP/1.1 request or status line: :method, :scheme, :authority and :path in requests, :status in responses. They must come before ordinary fields.

A mechanism that stops a sender from overrunning a receiver: the receiver grants credit (a window of bytes) and the sender may not exceed it until more is granted. HTTP/2 does this per stream and per connection, on top of TCP's own.
example: A 65,535-byte window over a 100 ms round trip caps one stream at about 5.24 Mbit/s.

definition: Extra meaningless bytes added to a message to hide its true length or align it to a block size.

A 2023 HTTP/2 denial-of-service attack in which clients opened streams with HEADERS and immediately cancelled them with RST_STREAM, so streams never counted as open for long while servers still began work on each request. Google reported a peak of about 398 million requests per second.
The RFC 9218 scheme that replaced HTTP/2's tree priorities with a simple priority header: u sets urgency from 0 (highest) to 7, default 3, and i marks a response that can be delivered incrementally.
example: priority: u=1, i asks for high urgency and incremental delivery.

definition: Google's web browser.

The header compression format for HTTP/2. It replaces repeated header fields with small indexes into a static table of 61 common fields and a per-connection dynamic table, and Huffman-codes literal strings.
example: :method: GET is encoded as the single byte 0x82.

definition: HPACK's fixed list of 61 common header fields, numbered from 1, that both sides know in advance. QPACK has its own static table of 99 entries.
example: Index 2 is :method: GET and index 7 is :scheme: https.

definition: The HPACK or QPACK table of recently used header fields that encoder and decoder build up identically during a connection. New entries go in at index 62 and the oldest are evicted when the size limit (default 4,096 bytes) would be exceeded.
A compression code that gives frequent symbols short bit patterns and rare ones long patterns. HPACK uses a fixed Huffman code tuned to header text, where common characters take 5 or 6 bits.
An HPACK representation in which a single integer refers to a whole name and value already in the static or dynamic table. Its first bit is 1.
example: 0x84 is index 4, :path: /.

definition: An HPACK representation that sends the value (and possibly the name) as a string. Variants add the field to the dynamic table, do not add it, or mark it never-indexed.

An HPACK representation that tells every hop, including proxies that re-encode headers, never to put this field into a compression table. It protects secrets such as short cookies or authorization tokens from compression side channels.

HPACK's integer format: a number that fits in the remaining N bits of a byte is stored there; otherwise those bits are all ones and the rest follows in 7-bit groups, each byte's top bit meaning more follows.
example: With a 5-bit prefix, 1337 is sent as the bytes 31, 154, 10.

definition: A 2012 attack showing that compressing secret data together with attacker-chosen data leaks the secret: the attacker guesses a value and watches whether the compressed size shrinks.
The request header that carries credentials such as a bearer token.

The header compression format for HTTP/3. Like HPACK it uses static and dynamic tables, but it sends table updates on dedicated unidirectional streams and lets each header block declare which entries it needs, avoiding head-of-line blocking between QUIC streams.
A unit of QUIC data inside a UDP datagram. Each packet has a header and an encrypted payload made of frames; one datagram can carry several coalesced packets.
One UDP message: an 8-byte header with ports, length and checksum, followed by the payload. UDP delivers each datagram whole or not at all, with no ordering or retransmission.

The kinds of frame carried in QUIC packets, including STREAM (stream data with an offset), ACK (acknowledged packet ranges), CRYPTO (TLS handshake bytes), MAX_DATA and MAX_STREAM_DATA (flow-control credit), NEW_CONNECTION_ID (spare connection IDs) and CONNECTION_CLOSE.
The QUIC packet header used during the handshake (first bit 1). It carries the version and both connection IDs with their lengths. Packet types are Initial, 0-RTT, Handshake and Retry.
The compact QUIC packet header (first bit 0) used for 1-RTT data once keys are available. After its first byte it carries only the Destination Connection ID and the packet number.

The first QUIC long-header packets, carrying the start of the TLS handshake. They are encrypted with keys anyone can derive from the Destination Connection ID and a published salt, so they give no confidentiality against anyone who can see them, though they make blind injection by off-path attackers harder.

Zero round-trip time data: application data a client sends in its first flight on a resumed connection, before the handshake completes. It can be replayed by an attacker, so it should carry only safe requests.
QUIC packets protected with the final handshake keys, sent with short headers; normal application data travels as 1-RTT.
Special QUIC long-header packets: Retry asks a client to repeat its Initial with a token proving its address, and Version Negotiation lists the QUIC versions a server supports.

The two connection IDs in a QUIC long header: the Destination Connection ID (DCID) chosen by the receiver of the packet, and the Source Connection ID (SCID) chosen by its sender. Short headers carry only the DCID. Because packets are matched to a connection by these IDs rather than by IP addresses and ports, a connection can survive an address change.
A number QUIC gives each packet, increasing and never reused within its packet number space. Because a retransmission goes in a new packet with a new number, ACKs are never ambiguous.
One of QUIC's three independent sequences of packet numbers: Initial, Handshake and application data. 0-RTT and 1-RTT packets share the application-data space.
One of QUIC's four sets of keys: Initial, 0-RTT, Handshake and 1-RTT.

QUIC encryption of the packet number and some low bits of the first header byte, using a mask computed from a sample of the encrypted payload and a separate header-protection key, so middleboxes cannot read or depend on those fields.
An optional bit in the QUIC short header that flips once per round trip, letting on-path observers estimate RTT. It is outside header protection.
A device on the network path that inspects or modifies traffic beyond plain routing, such as a firewall, NAT or load balancer. Middleboxes that depend on header details make protocols hard to change.

A value mixed into a hash or key-derivation function so that the same input produces different outputs in different contexts. QUIC version 1 publishes the salt it uses to derive Initial packet keys, so those keys are not secret.

QUIC's rule that, before it has validated a client's address, a server may send at most three times as many bytes as it received from that address. It limits how much traffic a spoofed packet can direct at a victim.
example: A 1,200-byte Initial allows at most 3,600 bytes in reply.

definition: Checking that a peer can really receive packets at the address it claims, by sending something unpredictable there and requiring it to be echoed back.
An attack in which the attacker sends requests with the victim's spoofed source address, so servers send their replies to the victim instead.

An integer encoding that uses fewer bytes for small numbers. QUIC varints put the total length (1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes) in the top two bits of the first byte, up to 2^62 − 1; protobuf varints instead carry 7 bits per byte, with the top bit meaning more bytes follow.
example: QUIC encodes 37 as the single byte 0x25; protobuf encodes 150 as 96 01.

definition: A bidirectional QUIC stream carries data both ways, like a request and its response; a unidirectional stream carries data one way only. HTTP/3 uses unidirectional streams for its control stream and QPACK.
Detecting lost packets and resending the information they carried. TCP resends bytes with their original sequence numbers; QUIC resends the needed frames in new packets.
The number TCP gives each byte of a stream. A retransmission reuses the same sequence numbers, so an ACK alone cannot tell which copy arrived.
TCP's rule of not taking round-trip-time samples from retransmitted segments, because their ACKs are ambiguous.
The time a receiver deliberately waits before sending an acknowledgement. QUIC reports it so the sender can subtract it from RTT samples.
A retransmission scheme that, after a loss, resends the lost item and everything sent after it. QUIC and modern TCP do not work this way.
An extension (RFC 9221) that lets QUIC carry unreliable application datagrams that are not retransmitted.

Moving a live QUIC connection to a new network path, such as from Wi-Fi to 5G, while keeping its keys and streams. It works because connections are identified by connection IDs rather than addresses; only the client may migrate actively.
A NAT assigning a new external port or address to an existing flow, often after it has been idle. To the server it looks like the client moved.
An extension letting one TCP connection use several network paths at once, such as Wi-Fi and cellular, and survive losing one.
Virtual private network: a tunnel that carries a device's traffic, usually encrypted, to another network so it appears to come from there.
A device moving its connection from one network or access point to another, such as from Wi-Fi to mobile data.
QUIC's check that a new address can receive packets: the endpoint sends a PATH_CHALLENGE with 8 random bytes and expects them echoed in a PATH_RESPONSE.
The sender-side algorithm that adjusts how much data is in flight to match what the network path can carry. Its state (the congestion window, cwnd) is reset after QUIC migrates to a new path.
A QUIC transport parameter in which a server offers a different address for the client to move to after the handshake.
A QUIC transport parameter by which an endpoint asks its peer not to migrate deliberately. It cannot stop NAT rebinding.
A design for load balancers that route QUIC packets by information encoded in connection IDs, so packets reach the same server even after the client's address changes.
A response header advertising that the same service is available another way, for example Alt-Svc: h3=":443" for HTTP/3 on UDP port 443.
A DNS record type (RFC 9460) that tells clients, before they connect, which protocols (such as alpn=h3) and addresses a service supports.
The family of IEEE 802.11 wireless local-network standards.
The fifth generation of mobile network technology.
A load balancer that chooses a backend from transport-layer information, such as the IP addresses and ports, without reading HTTP. It typically keeps every packet of one connection on one backend.
A proxy or load balancer that understands the application protocol, such as HTTP/2, and can route each request or stream separately.
One of the servers behind a load balancer or proxy that actually handles requests.
A group of 8 bits, the basic unit of data size. Network lengths and buffer sizes are counted in bytes.
example: A 9-byte HTTP/2 frame header is 72 bits.

definition: A binary digit, 0 or 1. Header fields are often described by their width in bits, and link speeds are given in bits per second.
A thousand bytes. KB is sometimes used loosely for 1,024 bytes; the unambiguous name for 1,024 bytes is a kibibyte (KiB).
A million bytes.
A thousand million (10^9) bytes.
example: A 4.7 GB file is 4,700,000,000 bytes.

definition: One thousandth of a second. Network round-trip times are usually tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
The fixed 12-byte start of every DNS query and response: six 16-bit fields holding the transaction ID, the flags word and four section counts.
example: The query for example.com begins with the 12 header bytes ab cd 01 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00.

definition: A number a client puts in a request so it can match the reply to it over a connectionless transport such as UDP. DNS uses a 16-bit ID (65,536 values) copied into the response; STUN uses a 96-bit one. A guessable ID makes forged replies easier.
example: A DNS query with ID 0xABCD is answered by a response that also carries 0xABCD.

definition: The 16-bit field after the DNS transaction ID that holds single-bit flags (QR, AA, TC, RD, RA, AD, CD), the 4-bit Opcode and the 4-bit RCODE.
example: Flags 0x8180 mean a response (QR=1) with recursion desired and available and RCODE 0.

definition: The top bit of the DNS flags word: 0 means the message is a query, 1 means it is a response.
example: A flags word starting with hex 8 has QR set, so it is a response.

definition: A 4-bit field in the DNS flags word saying what kind of query this is. It is almost always 0, a standard query.
example: In flags 0x0100 the Opcode bits are 0000: a standard query.

definition: A DNS flag set by a server that is authoritative for the name being asked about, meaning the answer comes from the zone itself rather than from a cache.
example: The name server for example.com sets AA when answering for www.example.com.

definition: A DNS flag meaning the response did not fit and was cut short. A resolver that sees it can repeat the query over TCP to get the full answer.
example: A 1,900-byte answer to a client without EDNS is returned truncated with TC set.

definition: A DNS flag set by the client to ask the server to chase the answer on its behalf. Stub clients on laptops and phones set it when asking their recursive resolver.
example: The example query flags 0x0100 have only RD set.

definition: A DNS flag set in a response when the server is willing to perform recursive lookups for this client.
example: A home router's resolver replies with RA=1.

definition: A DNS flag a resolver sets to say it validated the answer with DNSSEC. A client that does not validate itself has to trust the resolver and the path to it for this claim.
example: A validating resolver returns the signed A record for example.com with AD=1.

definition: A DNS flag a client sets to ask the resolver to return data even if DNSSEC validation fails, usually so the client can validate it itself.
example: With CD=0 a validating resolver returns SERVFAIL for bogus data; with CD=1 it can hand the data over.

definition: The originally reserved bits in the DNS flags word. Two of them were later given meanings for DNSSEC: AD (authenticated data) and CD (checking disabled).
example: In the flags diagram Z is the 3-bit field between RA and RCODE.

definition: The 4-bit response code at the end of the DNS flags word. 0 is NOERROR, 1 FORMERR, 2 SERVFAIL, 3 NXDOMAIN and 5 REFUSED.
example: Flags 0x8183 end in 0011, so RCODE is 3: NXDOMAIN.

definition: DNS RCODE 0: the query was processed without error. The answer section may still be empty if the name exists but has no record of the requested type.
example: Asking for the AAAA record of an IPv4-only name gives NOERROR with no answers.

definition: DNS RCODE 1, format error: the server could not interpret the query because it was malformed.
example: A query with a corrupt name encoding can get FORMERR.

definition: DNS RCODE 2, server failure: the server could not produce an answer. A validating resolver also returns it when DNSSEC validation fails.
example: A zone whose DS record points to a key that no longer exists makes validating resolvers return SERVFAIL.

definition: DNS RCODE 5: the server will not answer this query for policy reasons, for example because it does not provide recursion to this client.
example: An authoritative-only server answers a recursive query for an unrelated domain with REFUSED.

definition: The four 16-bit counts in the DNS header giving how many entries are in the question, answer, authority and additional sections.
example: A plain query has QDCOUNT 1 and the other three counts 0.

definition: The part of a DNS message after the header that states what is being asked: a name, a type (QTYPE) and a class (QCLASS).
example: The question for example.com A IN is 13 name bytes plus 4 bytes of type and class.

definition: The three record lists after the question in a DNS response. Answer holds records that answer the question, authority names the zone's name servers, and additional carries helpful extras such as those servers' addresses.
example: A referral has an empty answer section and NS records in the authority section.

definition: One dot-separated part of a domain name. On the wire each label is sent as a length byte followed by that many bytes, and a name ends with a zero-length root label. A label is at most 63 bytes.
example: www.example.com is sent as 03 www 07 example 03 com 00.

definition: The empty label, a single 00 byte, that ends every domain name on the wire. It stands for the root of the DNS tree.
example: The last byte of the encoded name example.com is the root label 00.

definition: The two 16-bit fields after the name in a DNS question: QTYPE is the record type asked for (1 for A) and QCLASS the class (1 for IN, the internet).
example: The example query ends 00 01 00 01: QTYPE A, QCLASS IN.

definition: One entry of DNS data: an owner name, a TYPE, a CLASS, a TTL in seconds, an RDLENGTH and the RDATA itself.
example: An A record for example.com with TTL 270 and a 4-byte IPv4 address is one resource record.

definition: The 16-bit field of a resource record that says what kind of data it holds, such as 1 for A, 28 for AAAA or 15 for MX.
example: 00 01 in a record's TYPE field means an A record.

definition: The 16-bit field of a resource record naming its protocol family. Almost everything uses 1, IN (internet).
example: 00 01 in the CLASS field means IN.

definition: The 16-bit field of a resource record giving the length in bytes of its RDATA, so a parser knows where the record ends.
example: An A record has RDLENGTH 4; an AAAA record has 16.

definition: The record-specific payload of a DNS resource record, for example the 4-byte IPv4 address of an A record or the host name of an MX record.
example: The RDATA of an AAAA record is a 16-byte IPv6 address.

definition: All the resource records with the same owner name, class and type, treated as one unit. DNSSEC signs whole RRsets, not single records.
example: The two MX records of bob.example form one RRset.

definition: The domain name a DNS resource record belongs to: the name it is about.
example: In bob.example. MX 10 mx1.bob.example., the owner name is bob.example.

definition: A 2-byte value in a DNS name whose top two bits are 11; the other 14 bits are an offset into the message where the rest of the name is found. It saves repeating names in a response.
example: c0 0c points to offset 12, where the question name starts.

definition: A malformed DNS message in which a compression pointer leads, directly or indirectly, back to itself. A careless parser follows it forever, so parsers must limit jumps and name length.
example: A pointer at offset 12 that points to offset 12 is a loop.

definition: A DNS resource record (type 1) holding one IPv4 address for a name. Its RDATA is 4 bytes.
example: example.com A 93.184.215.14 maps the name to an IPv4 address.

definition: A DNS resource record (type 28) holding one IPv6 address for a name. Its RDATA is 16 bytes.
example: example.com AAAA 2001:db8::1 maps the name to an IPv6 address.

definition: A DNS record holding free-form text strings. SPF policies, DKIM public keys and DMARC policies are all published as TXT records.
example: _dmarc.alice.example TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject" publishes a DMARC policy.

definition: The standard port number for DNS over both UDP and TCP.
example: A resolver retrying a truncated answer opens a TCP connection to port 53.

definition: The original maximum size of a DNS message over UDP. Without EDNS a server must not send more and sets TC instead.
example: A 1,900-byte answer cannot be sent in one classic UDP response.

definition: An extension to DNS that adds an OPT pseudo-record to a message so a client can advertise a larger UDP buffer and carry extra flags and options without changing the header.
example: A client advertising EDNS buffer size 1,232 can receive UDP answers up to 1,232 bytes.

definition: The pseudo-record that EDNS(0) adds to a DNS message's additional section. It is not real data: it carries the sender's UDP buffer size, flags such as DO and options such as cookies.
example: A query with no OPT record is limited to 512-byte UDP answers.

definition: A flag in the EDNS OPT record by which a client asks for DNSSEC records (signatures and keys) to be included in the response.
example: A validating resolver sets DO so authoritative servers return RRSIG records.

definition: The largest UDP DNS response a client says it can accept, advertised in its OPT record. DNS Flag Day 2020 recommended 1,232 bytes.
example: A buffer of 1,232 plus 40 bytes of IPv6 header and 8 of UDP header fits the 1,280-byte IPv6 minimum MTU.

definition: A coordinated 2020 change by DNS software vendors and operators that recommended a default EDNS buffer of 1,232 bytes, to avoid IP fragmentation of UDP answers.
example: After Flag Day 2020, larger answers fall back to TCP instead of being fragmented.

definition: Splitting one IP packet into several smaller pieces when it is larger than a link can carry. Fragments are often dropped by firewalls, and forged fragments can be used to tamper with DNS answers.
example: A 4,000-byte UDP DNS answer on a 1,500-byte-MTU path would be split into three fragments.

definition: Every IPv6 link must carry packets of at least 1,280 bytes, so a packet of that size or smaller should cross any IPv6 path without fragmentation.
example: 1,232 bytes of DNS + 8 of UDP + 40 of IPv6 header = 1,280.

definition: An EDNS option in which a recursive resolver passes part of the client's IP address to an authoritative server, so the answer can be tailored to the client's location.
example: A resolver might send 203.0.113.0/24 so a CDN can return a nearby server.

definition: Getting a forged DNS answer accepted into a resolver's cache, so later users of that resolver receive the attacker's data until it expires or is replaced.
example: If a resolver caches a fake A record for bank.example, its users are sent to the attacker's server.

definition: A DNS server that answers clients' questions by querying other servers on their behalf, from the root downwards, and caching the results. Your ISP, Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 and Google 8.8.8.8 run them.
example: A laptop asks its recursive resolver for example.com, which asks the root, .com and example.com's servers.

definition: The minimal DNS client in an operating system or app. It sends questions with RD set to a recursive resolver and does not chase referrals itself.
example: The resolver library on your phone is a stub resolver.

definition: A DNS server that holds the actual records for a zone and answers for it directly, rather than from a cache.
example: ns1.example.com is authoritative for example.com.

definition: An attacker who cannot see the traffic between two parties but can send forged packets to them. They must guess fields like IDs and ports instead of reading them.
example: An off-path attacker poisoning DNS has to guess the 16-bit transaction ID.

definition: An attacker positioned on the network path who can see, delay, drop or modify packets between two parties. Encryption and authentication are needed to defend against one.
example: Someone running a hostile Wi-Fi hotspot is on-path for everyone using it.

definition: A 2008 DNS cache-poisoning technique by Dan Kaminsky. The attacker makes a resolver look up fresh random names (x71.bank.example, x72...) and races forged responses that claim a new name server for the whole zone, so failures cost no TTL wait.
example: With 100 guesses per attempt, about 454 attempts give a 50% chance of a correct ID in the simple model.

definition: Sending each DNS query from a randomly chosen UDP source port, so an off-path attacker must guess the port as well as the 16-bit ID. It was the emergency fix after the Kaminsky attack.
example: With 28,000 possible ports and 65,536 IDs there are about 1.8 billion combinations.

definition: The port number on the sending side of a TCP or UDP packet. A reply is sent back to it.
example: A resolver sending from port 54,211 accepts answers only addressed to 54,211.

definition: A temporary port number the operating system picks for the client side of a connection or query, from a configured range such as 32768–60999 on Linux.
example: Each new outgoing DNS query can use a different ephemeral port.

definition: A resolver rule that only accepts records from a response if they fall within the authority of the server that sent it. A server for bank.example cannot plant records for google.com.
example: Records for google.com in a response about x71.bank.example are discarded as out of bailiwick.

definition: Randomising the upper and lower case of letters in a DNS query name and checking the server echoes it exactly. Each letter adds one bit for an off-path attacker to guess. Its name comes from 0x20, the bit that differs between upper and lower case in ASCII.
example: A query for wWw.ExAmPlE.cOm only accepts an answer with exactly that case.

definition: An EDNS option (RFC 7873) in which client and server exchange short secret values, so forged responses from an off-path attacker who does not know them can be detected.
example: A resolver that sent a client cookie rejects a response that does not echo it.

definition: A 2020 attack that used a side channel, Linux's global rate limit on ICMP port-unreachable replies, to discover which source port a resolver was using, reducing poisoning to guessing the 16-bit ID again.
example: By counting missing ICMP replies the attacker could test thousands of ports per second.

definition: Information leaked indirectly by how a system behaves (timing, error counts, sizes) rather than by the data it intends to send.
example: SAD DNS learned an open port from how many ICMP errors a server sent back.

definition: Internet Control Message Protocol: the protocol IP hosts and routers use to report errors and diagnostics, such as "port unreachable" or the replies to ping.
example: Sending UDP to a closed port normally triggers an ICMP port unreachable message.

definition: An ICMP error message a host sends when a UDP packet arrives for a port on which nothing is listening.
example: A probe to a closed UDP port returns ICMP port unreachable.

definition: DNS Security Extensions: digital signatures on DNS data, checked along a chain of keys from the root, so a validating resolver can detect forged or altered answers. It provides authenticity and integrity, not privacy.
example: A signed A record for example.com comes with an RRSIG that the resolver verifies.

definition: A DNSSEC record holding one of a zone's public keys, used to verify that zone's signatures.
example: example.com publishes its KSK and ZSK as two DNSKEY records.

definition: A DNSSEC record holding a signature over one RRset, with an inception and expiry time. A validator checks it with the zone's DNSKEY.
example: The A RRset for www.example.com is accompanied by an RRSIG.

definition: Delegation Signer: a DNSSEC record published in the parent zone that holds a key tag, algorithm and digest identifying one of the child zone's DNSKEYs. It links the chain of trust from parent to child.
example: The .com zone holds a DS for example.com that matches example.com's KSK.

definition: A DNSSEC record that names the next existing name in a zone's sorted order and the types present, so a signed answer can prove a name or type does not exist.
example: alpha.example.com NSEC delta.example.com proves charlie.example.com does not exist.

definition: A variant of NSEC that chains hashes of names instead of the names themselves, making zone walking slower. The hashes can still be attacked offline with dictionaries of guessed names.
example: An NSEC3 record covers a range of hashed names rather than alpha to delta.

definition: DNSSEC's way of proving with signatures that a name or record type does not exist, using NSEC or NSEC3 records.
example: A signed NXDOMAIN for charlie.example.com includes NSEC records covering the gap.

definition: Listing all the names in a DNSSEC-signed zone by following its NSEC chain from one name to the next.
example: Asking for names just after each NSEC target reveals alpha, delta, kilo and so on.

definition: A part of the DNS name space managed as one unit by one operator, such as example.com, with its own name servers and records.
example: bank.example is a zone; x71.bank.example is a name inside it.

definition: In a split-key DNSSEC setup, the key that signs the zone's DNSKEY RRset. The parent's DS record points to it, so changing it needs a DS update at the parent.
example: Re-signing example.com with a new KSK without updating .com's DS breaks validation.

definition: In a split-key DNSSEC setup, the key that signs the zone's ordinary RRsets. It can be rolled without involving the parent zone.
example: The A and MX RRsets of example.com are signed by its ZSK.

definition: A public key a validator trusts in advance, configured rather than looked up. DNSSEC validation chains every answer back to the root zone's trust anchor.
example: Validating resolvers ship with the root KSK as their trust anchor.

definition: The sequence root key → DS → child DNSKEY → … → RRSIG by which a validator links a signed answer back to its trust anchor. Any broken link makes the data bogus.
example: root → .com DS → .com DNSKEY → example.com DS → example.com DNSKEY → A RRSIG.

definition: The DNSSEC state of data whose signatures should validate but do not, for example because they expired or the DS points to a missing key. A validating resolver returns SERVFAIL for it.
example: Forgetting to update the DS after a KSK change makes the zone bogus.

definition: A child zone that the parent proves, with signatures, has no DS record. Its data is treated as unsigned rather than bogus, so it is returned without the AD bit.
example: An unsigned zone under signed .com is insecure, not broken.

definition: Checking DNSSEC signatures on an answer along the chain of trust. A resolver or stub that does this is a validator.
example: A validator rejects an A record whose RRSIG expired yesterday.

definition: Replacing a DNSSEC key with a new one in carefully timed steps, so that caches always hold a key and DS combination that validates.
example: A KSK rollover publishes the new key, updates the parent DS, waits for caches, then removes the old key.

definition: A 16-bit checksum of a DNSKEY used to pick which key a signature or DS refers to. It is not unique, so several keys can share one.
example: KeyTrap used many keys with the same key tag to force extra signature checks.

definition: A 2024 denial-of-service vulnerability in DNSSEC validators: crafted zones with many colliding key tags and signatures forced vulnerable resolvers to try huge numbers of combinations.
example: Patched resolvers now cap how many keys and signatures they try per answer.

definition: A DDoS technique: the attacker sends small requests with a forged source address so a server sends much larger replies to the victim.
example: A 60-byte DNS query that triggers a 3,000-byte signed answer amplifies traffic about 50 times.

definition: Distributed denial of service: overwhelming a service with traffic or work from many sources so legitimate users cannot reach it. DoS is the single-source form.
example: A botnet flooding a resolver with queries is a DDoS attack.

definition: An elliptic-curve digital signature algorithm (DNSSEC algorithm 13). Its signatures are 64 bytes, far smaller than the 256 bytes of RSA-2048, which keeps signed DNS answers small.
example: Switching a zone from RSA-2048 to algorithm 13 cuts each RRSIG's signature from 256 to 64 bytes.

definition: RSA with a 2,048-bit key. Its signatures are 256 bytes long.
example: A DNSSEC RRSIG made with RSA-2048 carries a 256-byte signature.

definition: Sending ordinary DNS messages, each with a 2-byte length prefix, inside a TLS connection to port 853 (RFC 7858). It hides queries from the network but its own port makes it easy to block.
example: Android's Private DNS setting uses DoT.

definition: Sending DNS messages as HTTPS requests (RFC 8484), usually to port 443, with media type application/dns-message. It blends in with web traffic more than DoT.
example: Firefox can send its lookups to a DoH resolver instead of the network's DNS server.

definition: Sending DNS messages over dedicated QUIC connections on UDP port 853 (RFC 9250).
example: A DoQ client avoids TCP's head-of-line blocking between queries.

definition: An experimental DoH design (RFC 9230) that sends encrypted queries through a proxy, so the proxy sees the client but not the query and the resolver sees the query but not the client, as long as the two do not collude.
example: A proxy run by one company relays queries to a resolver run by another.

definition: The HTTP media type for a binary DNS message carried in a DoH request or response.
example: A DoH POST has Content-Type: application/dns-message.

definition: A variant of base64 that encodes binary data as text using only letters, digits, - and _, so it can appear safely in URLs.
example: A DoH GET puts the DNS message base64url-encoded in /dns-query?dns=....

definition: Server Name Indication: the host name a client sends in plaintext at the start of a TLS handshake so the server can pick the right certificate. It reveals which site you are visiting.
example: Even with DoH, an observer can read bank.example in the SNI unless ECH is used.

definition: A TLS extension that encrypts the sensitive parts of the client's first handshake message, including SNI, so an observer cannot read the site name. It is specified in RFC 9849 (2026).
example: With ECH, a network sees only the provider's public name instead of the real site.

definition: Internet service provider: the company that connects you to the internet, and whose resolver you use by default.
example: Switching to DoH moves your DNS trust from your ISP to the DoH provider.

definition: A special domain a network can make fail on purpose to signal "do not enable DoH here". Firefox checks use-application-dns.net before turning DoH on automatically.
example: A school network returns NXDOMAIN for use-application-dns.net to keep its filtering.

definition: Internationalising Domain Names in Applications: the rules for converting names with non-ASCII characters into ASCII "xn--" labels that DNS can carry.
example: bücher.example becomes xn--bcher-kva.example on the wire.

definition: A 7-bit character code covering English letters, digits and punctuation, one byte per character. DNS labels are ASCII on the wire.
example: The letter a is ASCII 0x61 and A is 0x41.

definition: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: the line-based text protocol that moves email from clients to servers and between servers (RFC 5321).
example: A server opens with 220, and the client says EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO and DATA.

definition: Extended SMTP: SMTP with extensions such as STARTTLS, SIZE and 8BITMIME, negotiated when the client greets with EHLO.
example: 220 mx1.bob.example ESMTP tells the client the server supports extensions.

definition: The email program a person uses to read and write mail, such as Outlook, Apple Mail or Thunderbird.
example: Alice's MUA submits her message to her provider on port 587.

definition: The server that accepts new mail from authenticated users' mail clients, on port 587 or 465, before it is relayed onwards.
example: Alice's provider runs an MSA that checks her password before accepting mail.

definition: A mail server that relays messages to other mail servers using SMTP, usually on port 25.
example: Alice's provider's MTA looks up bob.example's MX and connects to it.

definition: The software that puts a received message into the recipient's mailbox.
example: Bob's provider's MDA files the message into his INBOX.

definition: Handing a new message from a mail client to the sender's own provider, after authenticating, on port 587 (STARTTLS) or 465 (implicit TLS).
example: Phones send mail by submission, not by relaying straight to the recipient.

definition: Passing a message from one mail server to another with SMTP, usually on port 25.
example: Alice's provider relays to mx1.bob.example on port 25.

definition: The standard port for server-to-server SMTP relay. Many home ISPs block outgoing connections to it to stop infected computers sending spam.
example: A laptop on home broadband often cannot connect to any server on port 25.

definition: The standard mail submission port, where a client connects in plaintext and upgrades with STARTTLS before authenticating.
example: smtplib.SMTP(host, 587) followed by starttls() is classic submission.

definition: The mail submission port that uses implicit TLS: TLS starts as soon as the connection opens. RFC 8314 recommends it.
example: smtplib.SMTP_SSL(host, 465) speaks TLS from the first byte.

definition: A DNS record naming a mail server for a domain, with a preference number. Senders try the lowest preference number first.
example: bob.example MX 10 mx1.bob.example makes mx1 the preferred mail server.

definition: The number in an MX record that orders mail servers: lower numbers are tried first, and servers with equal numbers are chosen between randomly.
example: MX 10 is tried before MX 20.

definition: The fallback when a domain has no MX records at all: senders deliver to the domain's own A or AAAA address.
example: A domain with only an A record still receives mail at that address.

definition: An MX record with preference 0 and target "." (RFC 7505) meaning "this domain accepts no mail", so senders fail immediately instead of retrying for days.
example: noreply.example MX 0 . stops all delivery attempts.

definition: A command that upgrades an existing plaintext connection (SMTP, IMAP, POP3) to TLS. Because the offer is sent in plaintext, an on-path attacker can strip it unless TLS is required by policy.
example: After 250-STARTTLS the client sends STARTTLS and starts the TLS handshake.

definition: Starting TLS immediately when a connection opens, before any protocol commands, on a dedicated port such as 465, 993 or 995.
example: IMAP on port 993 uses implicit TLS.

definition: Using TLS if the other side offers it but falling back to plaintext if not. It protects against passive eavesdroppers but an active attacker can strip the offer.
example: Most server-to-server mail uses opportunistic STARTTLS on port 25.

definition: Forcing a connection to use a weaker option, for example by deleting the STARTTLS offer so mail goes in plaintext.
example: An attacker removes 250-STARTTLS from the EHLO reply and reads the message.

definition: The SMTP greeting a client sends to start an extended session. The server replies with the extensions it supports.
example: EHLO mail.alice.example gets back 250-SIZE, 250-STARTTLS and 250 8BITMIME.

definition: The original SMTP greeting, without extensions. The domain name the client gives in it (or in EHLO) is checked by SPF when the envelope sender is empty.
example: A bounce with MAIL FROM:<> is SPF-checked against the HELO name.

definition: An SMTP extension by which a server advertises the largest message it will accept, in bytes.
example: 250-SIZE 52428800 means messages up to 52,428,800 bytes (50 MiB).

definition: An SMTP extension saying the server accepts message bodies containing bytes above 127, not just 7-bit ASCII.
example: A server listing 250 8BITMIME accepts UTF-8 text without re-encoding.

definition: The SMTP command giving the envelope sender (return path): the address bounces go to. It can differ from the From: header.
example: MAIL FROM:<bounces@alice.example> sends bounces to a dedicated address.

definition: The SMTP command naming one envelope recipient. Delivery follows these commands, not the To: header.
example: A Bcc recipient appears only in an RCPT TO command.

definition: The SMTP command after which the client sends the message itself (headers and body), ending with a line containing just a dot.
example: The server answers DATA with 354 and waits for the message.

definition: The three-digit number at the start of every SMTP server reply. The first digit matters most: 2 success, 3 continue, 4 temporary failure (retry later), 5 permanent failure.
example: 451 means try again later; 550 means do not retry unchanged.

definition: An SMTP 4xx reply: the sender should keep the message queued and retry later, typically for at least 4–5 days before giving up.
example: 451 4.7.1 Try again later keeps the message in the sender's queue.

definition: A second, dotted code after an SMTP reply code, such as 4.7.1, that gives a more precise reason (class.subject.detail).
example: In 451 4.7.1, the 4.7.1 means a temporary security or policy refusal.

definition: Where an MTA keeps messages it has not yet delivered, retrying them on a schedule until they succeed or expire.
example: A message deferred with 451 sits in the queue and is retried after some minutes.

definition: An anti-spam technique where a server temporarily rejects mail from an unfamiliar sender with a 4xx code, accepting it when the sender retries. Much spamware never retries.
example: A first attempt gets 451; the retry ten minutes later is accepted.

definition: An automatic message sent back to the envelope sender saying a message could not be delivered. It is sent with an empty envelope sender, MAIL FROM:<>.
example: Mail to a nonexistent mailbox produces a bounce to the return path.

definition: An empty envelope sender, MAIL FROM:<>, used for bounces so that a failed bounce never generates another bounce.
example: A delivery failure notice is sent with MAIL FROM:<>.

definition: The addresses given in SMTP commands, MAIL FROM and RCPT TO, that decide who gets the message and where bounces go. They are separate from the From: and To: headers a mail client displays.
example: A mailing list keeps your From: but sets its own envelope sender.

definition: The address in MAIL FROM, also called the return path: where bounces are sent and the domain SPF checks. It can differ from the visible From: address.
example: Newsletters often use bounce@mail.shop.example as the envelope sender.

definition: The lines at the top of an email message (RFC 5322), such as From:, To:, Cc:, Subject: and Date:. The mail client displays them; delivery does not depend on them.
example: From: Alice <alice@alice.example> is what Bob sees as the sender.

definition: Blind carbon copy: a recipient who gets the message without being listed to the others. Typically their address is only in RCPT TO and the Bcc header is removed.
example: Carol, Bcc'd, receives a message that appears to be addressed only to Bob.

definition: A service that redistributes each message sent to it to many subscribers. Lists often change the subject or add footers, which breaks DKIM signatures.
example: A list adds [team] to the subject and a footer before resending.

definition: The SMTP rule that a body line starting with "." is sent with an extra dot, so it cannot be mistaken for the line containing just "." that ends the message. The receiver removes the extra dot.
example: A body line ".hidden" is sent as "..hidden".

definition: The sequence CR LF . CR LF that ends a message in SMTP: a line containing only a dot.
example: The client sends "." on its own line and the server replies 250 OK queued.

definition: A 2023 attack in which servers disagreed about the end-of-data sequence (for example accepting a bare LF.LF), letting an attacker hide a second, forged message inside the first that the receiver treated as coming from the sending provider.
example: A message containing <LF>.<LF>MAIL FROM:... is split into two by a vulnerable receiver.

definition: Carriage return (CR, byte 0x0D) and line feed (LF, byte 0x0A): the two control characters that together end a line in SMTP. A bare LF is one without the CR before it.
example: \r\n is CR LF; \n alone is a bare LF.

definition: SMTP MTA Strict Transport Security (RFC 8461): a domain publishes over HTTPS a policy saying senders must use authenticated TLS to its listed MX hosts, so STARTTLS cannot be stripped once the policy is cached.
example: A sender with alice.example's enforce policy refuses to deliver in plaintext.

definition: DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities: publishing in DNSSEC-signed TLSA records which certificates or keys a server may use, so senders can require and verify TLS without a CA (RFC 7672 for SMTP).
example: A TLSA record at _25._tcp.mx1.bob.example pins mx1's certificate.

definition: A DNS record used by DANE that states which certificate or public key is valid for a TLS service at a given port and name.
example: _25._tcp.mx1.bob.example TLSA 3 1 1 <hash> pins the server's key.

definition: Post Office Protocol version 3: a simple protocol for downloading mail from a server (port 110, or 995 with TLS), traditionally deleting it afterwards.
example: An old phone app downloads new messages by POP3 every 15 minutes.

definition: Internet Message Access Protocol: keeps mail on the server and lets many clients view, search, flag and move it, staying in sync (port 143, or 993 with TLS). The current version is IMAP4rev2, RFC 9051.
example: Reading a message on your phone marks it read on your laptop too.

definition: The standard port for IMAP over implicit TLS.
example: A mail app connects to imap.example.com:993.

definition: A short label such as a1 the client puts before each IMAP command; the server ends its reply with the same tag so responses can be matched to commands.
example: C: a2 SELECT INBOX is answered by S: a2 OK ... SELECT done.

definition: An IMAP server line starting with * instead of a tag: data or a notification, such as the message count, rather than the end of a command.
example: * 172 EXISTS tells the client the mailbox holds 172 messages.

definition: A message's position in an IMAP mailbox, from 1 upwards. It changes when an earlier message is expunged, so it is not a stable identifier.
example: After message 3 is expunged, message 4 becomes message 3.

definition: A message's unique identifier in an IMAP mailbox. It never changes or gets reused while the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY stays the same, so clients cache by it.
example: UID FETCH 4827 fetches the same message every session.

definition: A number an IMAP server reports for each mailbox. If it changes, all previously cached UIDs for that mailbox are invalid and the client must resynchronise.
example: A stored UIDVALIDITY 3857529045 that comes back different means the mailbox was rebuilt.

definition: Permanently removing messages marked \Deleted from an IMAP mailbox. Marking alone does not remove them.
example: Set \Deleted on message 5, then EXPUNGE removes it.

definition: Markers stored on the server for each IMAP message, such as \Seen (read), \Flagged (starred) and \Deleted (marked for removal). They sync across all clients.
example: Reading a message on one device sets \Seen for all.

definition: An IMAP command that keeps the connection open so the server can push mailbox changes, such as new mail, as they happen. Clients reissue it periodically because connections time out.
example: A phone in IDLE learns of new mail within seconds.

definition: The IMAP command that opens a mailbox for reading and writing; the server replies with its message count, UIDVALIDITY and other state.
example: a2 SELECT INBOX opens the inbox.

definition: The IMAP command that retrieves parts of messages, such as flags, headers or the body. UID FETCH addresses messages by UID instead of sequence number.
example: a3 UID FETCH 4827 (FLAGS BODY[]) gets flags and full content.

definition: The special IMAP mailbox where new mail arrives. Its name is case-insensitive.
example: a2 SELECT INBOX opens the user's main mailbox.

definition: The IMAP command that authenticates with a username and password; it should only be used over TLS.
example: a1 LOGIN bob secret authenticates Bob.

definition: JSON Meta Application Protocol (RFC 8620): a synchronisation framework using JSON over HTTP, with JMAP Mail (RFC 8621) as a modern alternative to IMAP.
example: A web client asks a JMAP server for changes since its last state string.

definition: Sender Policy Framework (RFC 7208): a domain publishes a TXT record listing the IP addresses allowed to send mail using it as envelope sender. Receivers check the connecting IP against it.
example: v=spf1 ip4:192.0.2.0/24 -all allows only that /24 range.

definition: The final term of an SPF record, giving the result for IPs not listed: -all means fail, ~all softfail (suspicious) and ?all neutral (no opinion).
example: A record ending -all tells receivers unlisted IPs fail SPF.

definition: An SPF mechanism that also authorises the IPs listed in another domain's SPF record, such as a mail provider's. Each one counts towards the ten-lookup limit.
example: include:_spf.google.com authorises Google Workspace servers.

definition: SPF allows at most ten evaluated terms that cause DNS queries (include, a, mx, ptr, exists, redirect) across a whole check. Going over gives permerror.
example: Five includes, four nested terms, mx and a make eleven: permerror.

definition: A permanent SPF error, for example a syntax error or exceeding the ten-lookup limit. It does not count as an SPF pass for DMARC.
example: An SPF record with too many includes always returns permerror.

definition: The IP address of the server that opened the SMTP connection to the receiver. SPF checks whether it is authorised.
example: Mail forwarded by a university arrives from the university's connecting IP.

definition: A way of writing a block of IP addresses as an address and a prefix length: 192.0.2.0/24 covers the 256 addresses that share the first 24 bits.
Automatically resending received mail to another address. The forwarder's IP is not in the original sender's SPF record, so SPF often fails after forwarding.
example: bob@uni.example forwarding to Gmail makes Gmail see the university's IP.

definition: DomainKeys Identified Mail (RFC 6376): the sending server signs selected headers and the body and adds a DKIM-Signature header; receivers verify it with a public key published in DNS.
example: d=alice.example; s=mail2026 tells the receiver to fetch mail2026._domainkey.alice.example.

definition: The header added by a DKIM signer. Its tags give the version (v=), algorithm (a=), canonicalisation (c=), signing domain (d=), selector (s=), signed headers (h=), body hash (bh=) and signature (b=).
example: a=rsa-sha256 means an RSA signature over a SHA-256 hash.

definition: The s= tag naming which of a domain's DKIM keys signed the message; the key is published at <selector>._domainkey.<domain>. Several selectors let a domain run several keys at once.
example: s=mail2026 points to mail2026._domainkey.alice.example.

definition: The d= tag of a DKIM signature: the domain that takes responsibility for the message. DMARC checks whether it aligns with the From: domain.
example: A SaaS signing with d=invoicer.example does not align with From: billing@corp.example.

definition: The bh= tag of a DKIM signature: a hash of the canonicalised message body (or the prefix chosen by l=). Any covered change to the body makes it mismatch.
example: A mailing list adding a footer changes the body hash.

definition: Normalising a message before hashing so harmless changes do not break a DKIM signature. relaxed mode tidies whitespace and header-name case; simple tolerates almost nothing.
example: With relaxed, "Subject:  Hi" and "subject: Hi" hash the same.

definition: The part of an email or HTTP header before the colon, such as Subject in "Subject: Lunch?". In email it is case-insensitive.
example: "subject" and "Subject" are the same field name.

definition: An optional DKIM tag limiting the body hash to the first l bytes. Content appended after that prefix is not covered by the signature, which is a risk.
example: With l=500, a footer added after byte 500 does not break the signature.

definition: The size of a DKIM RSA key in bits. RFC 8301 requires at least 1024 bits and recommends at least 2048.
example: A 512-bit DKIM key is too weak and should be rejected.

definition: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance: a policy at _dmarc.<domain> saying a message passes only if SPF or DKIM passes for a domain aligned with the visible From:, and what receivers should do otherwise. RFC 9989 (2026) replaces RFC 7489.
example: _dmarc.alice.example TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject" asks receivers to reject failing mail.

definition: DMARC's requirement that the domain SPF or DKIM authenticated matches the visible From: domain: the same organisational domain in relaxed mode, exactly the same in strict mode.
example: promo.shop.example aligns with shop.example in relaxed mode but not strict.

definition: The registered domain an organisation controls, such as shop.example for promo.shop.example. DMARC relaxed alignment compares organisational domains; RFC 9989 finds them with a DNS tree walk.
example: mail.alice.example and alice.example share organisational domain alice.example.

definition: The two DMARC alignment modes. Relaxed (default) accepts subdomains of the same organisational domain; strict (aspf=s for SPF, adkim=s for DKIM) needs an exact domain match.
example: With aspf=s, an SPF pass for promo.shop.example does not align with shop.example.

definition: The p= tag of a DMARC record asking receivers how to treat failing mail: none (monitor only), quarantine (treat as suspicious, e.g. spam folder) or reject (refuse it). Receivers may override it.
example: Moving from p=none to p=reject before all senders align rejects legitimate mail.

definition: A periodic summary, requested with the rua= tag, that receivers send to a domain owner listing which IPs sent mail using the domain and whether SPF, DKIM and DMARC passed.
example: Reports reveal an invoicing SaaS sending as corp.example without alignment.

definition: Sending mail that claims to come from someone else's address, usually in the From: header. Phishing uses it to impersonate banks and colleagues.
example: A phisher sends From: <it@alice.example> from their own server.

definition: Authenticated Received Chain (RFC 8617): each forwarder records the authentication results it saw and signs them, so a final receiver that trusts the forwarder can accept mail whose SPF and DKIM broke in transit.
example: A mailing list adds ARC seals saying DKIM passed on arrival.

definition: A sender of large volumes of mail. Gmail requires senders of around 5,000 or more messages a day to personal accounts to use SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
example: A newsletter sending 20,000 messages a day to Gmail must publish DMARC.

definition: A List-Unsubscribe mechanism (RFC 8058) that lets a recipient unsubscribe with a single click in the mail client, without visiting a website.
example: Gmail shows an Unsubscribe link next to the sender for compliant mailings.

definition: Software as a service: software run by a vendor and used over the internet, such as an invoicing or marketing tool that sends mail on your behalf.
example: An invoicing SaaS sending as billing@corp.example needs aligned DKIM.

definition: Python's standard-library module for speaking SMTP as a client.
example: smtplib.SMTP(host, 587) opens a submission connection.

definition: Microsoft's hosted office suite, including Exchange Online email for organisations.
example: A company's staff mail is sent by its Microsoft 365 tenant.

definition: One customer's separate account and data inside a shared hosted service.
example: corp.example's Microsoft 365 tenant is isolated from other companies'.

definition: Network Time Protocol: the protocol computers use to set their clocks from time servers over the network. Version 4 runs over UDP port 123.
example: A laptop's NTP client queries a pool server every few minutes and nudges its clock to stay within milliseconds of UTC.

definition: An NTP server's distance from a reference clock. Stratum 1 servers attach directly to a reference clock, stratum 2 servers sync from stratum 1, and so on; stratum 16 means unsynchronised.
example: A server syncing from a GPS-attached stratum 1 server reports itself as stratum 2.

definition: A highly accurate time source, such as a GPS receiver or an atomic clock, that a stratum 1 NTP server reads directly. It is informally called stratum 0.
example: A stratum 1 server in a data centre may take its time from a GPS antenna on the roof.

definition: NTP's estimate of how far the server's clock is ahead of the client's clock, computed from four timestamps. A positive offset means the client is behind and should move forward.
example: With t1 = 10.000, t2 = 10.150, t3 = 10.152 and t4 = 10.042 seconds, the offset is 0.130 s: the client is 130 ms behind.

definition: In NTP, the total time a request and its response spent on the network: the client's elapsed time minus the time the server spent processing. It bounds how wrong one offset measurement can be.
example: If 41 ms pass on the client and the server held the request for 1 ms, the delay is 40 ms.

definition: When the trip from client to server takes a different time from the trip back. NTP assumes both directions are equal, so asymmetry biases its offset estimate by half the difference.
example: A 5 ms outbound and 35 ms return trip makes NTP's offset wrong by (5 − 35) / 2 = −15 ms.

definition: The four times recorded in one NTP exchange: t1 when the client sends, t2 when the server receives, t3 when the server replies and t4 when the client receives. t1 and t4 come from the client's clock, t2 and t3 from the server's.
The gradual gain or loss of time by a clock whose oscillator runs slightly fast or slow. It is usually quoted in parts per million.
example: A clock drifting at 20 ppm gains or loses about 1.7 seconds a day.

definition: A ratio of one in a million, used to express how fast or slow a clock runs. 1 ppm is one microsecond of error per second of real time.
example: 20 ppm × 86,400 seconds in a day ≈ 1.7 seconds of error per day.
